article.overview: This article covers X-ray spectrometers as a measurement class: instruments that record the energies and intensities of X-rays emitted by a planetary surface so that its elemental composition can be inferred. On the Moon, the main method is X-ray fluorescence (XRF). Sunlight, especially its X-ray component during solar flares, excites atoms in the regolith, and each element emits X-rays at characteristic energies. Four flown lunar examples are described, all in lunar orbit: the Chandrayaan-1 X-ray Spectrometer (C1XS), the SMART-1 Demonstration of a Compact X-ray Spectrometer (D-CIXS), the Chandrayaan-2 Large Area Soft X-ray Spectrometer (CLASS), and the X-ray Spectrometer (XRS) on SELENE (Kaguya). In scope: X-ray spectrometers used for remote, orbital elemental mapping of the lunar surface, and their companion solar X-ray monitors. Cross-referenced rather than duplicated: the Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS, entry 054), a contact instrument; the general X-ray fluorescence spectrometer (entry 055), which should be the primary article for the XRF technique; the gamma-ray spectrometer (entry 057); and the neutron spectrometer (entry 058). The boundary with entry 055 is provisional because that article had not been generated when this article was written. No image in this article has been verified as a direct asset URL in this run, so no images are embedded.
article.description: An X-ray spectrometer measures how many X-ray photons arrive at a detector in each energy channel. Each element emits X-rays at energies characteristic of its atomic structure, so the spectrum identifies which elements are present. The line intensities depend on how much of each element is present, on the excitation conditions and on the instrument's response, so a calibrated measurement is needed to derive abundances. For lunar XRF the excitation is solar X-ray radiation, which varies strongly, so the instruments depend on a companion solar monitor. Chandrayaan-1 C1XS is paired with an X-ray Solar Monitor (XSM) whose solar spectra are used to derive absolute elemental abundances [1][2]. SELENE XRS had a companion solar monitor, SOL-BC [9]. SMART-1 D-CIXS was paired with an X-ray Solar Monitor used to calibrate its lunar and cruise data [3]. The detectors are swept charge devices (SCDs), one-dimensional X-ray CCD-type detectors, or CCD arrays in SELENE XRS. The sources describe these detectors as suited to the soft X-ray band of roughly 1 to 7 keV, where the fluorescence lines of the major rock-forming elements (Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti and Fe) lie [1][7][9].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar X-ray spectrometer is global or regional elemental mapping of the surface from orbit. C1XS was built to map major rock-forming elements such as Mg, Al, Si, Ti, Ca and Fe [1]. D-CIXS was intended to produce the first global view of the lunar surface in X-ray fluorescence, with elemental abundances of Fe, Mg, Al and Si [3][4][6]. CLASS aims to produce global maps of O, Mg, Al and Si at a stated resolution of 12.5 km per pixel, and of Ca, Ti and Fe in localised regions during enhanced solar activity [7]. SELENE XRS was meant to map Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti and Fe [8][9]. Elemental ratios such as Mg/Si or Al/Si are used in lunar geochemistry to distinguish rock types and study the crust; the sources accessed support this general use, but no specific geochemical result from the examples is reproduced here. Because XRF is driven by solar X-rays, CLASS was designed to use flare events for some elements [7], so solar activity is part of the scientific scope and not only an operational constraint.
article.operating_principle: An X-ray spectrometer for lunar XRF has four connected parts. (1) Excitation: solar X-rays strike the top layer of the regolith and eject inner-shell electrons from surface atoms. (2) Emission: electron vacancies are filled by outer-shell electrons, and each transition emits an X-ray whose energy is characteristic of the element; this is the fluorescence signal. (3) Collimation and detection: a collimator defines the ground field of view, and a detector records each photon's energy, with energy resolution determining how well neighbouring lines are separated. C1XS uses micromachined collimators and a 14 degree FWHM field of view, equivalent to a footprint of about 25 km from 100 km altitude [1]. CLASS uses a gold-coated copper collimator with a field of view of about 14 degrees and a ground pixel of about 25 km by 25 km (FWHM) from its orbit [7]. (4) Solar reference: a separate solar monitor measures the incident solar X-ray spectrum so that the lunar fluorescence can be normalised to the excitation actually received [1][3][9]. The measured spectrum is fitted for element-line intensities, and the calibrated intensities are converted to abundances using calibration data and a surface model. The sources accessed do not give one universal conversion procedure.
article.scientific_importance: XRF is one of the few techniques that can map major elemental composition from orbit. Infrared and visible spectrometers see mineral absorptions, but many rock-forming elements have no simple optical signature, so orbital XRF complements other compositional measurements. The sources report that these instruments had difficulty meeting their solar-dependent goals. The C1XS mission record reports that solar X-ray activity was sparse and that C1XS saw only about 30 solar X-ray bursts, which limited global mapping [5]. The SELENE XRS mapping goal was not met; later reports attribute this to instrumental trouble and a historically quiet solar X-ray flux [8][9]. CLASS has been measuring lunar XRF since September 2019 and was designed partly for flare-driven observations [7][10]. The scientific value of these instruments therefore depends on both instrument performance and the Sun's activity during each mission.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an X-ray spectrometer. The examples differ in mission, orbit, detector technology, energy range and development stage, so their numbers should not be ranked against one another. Each value is tied to the named instrument and source. Where a source does not publish a value, the text states 'not publicly specified in the sources accessed' and no value is inferred. Several sources conflict for some parameters; these conflicts are recorded in each example and in data_quality_notes rather than resolved.

The RAL Space mission summary reports that the mission ended in late August 2009 after a major spacecraft failure [5]. Built by the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) [1][2].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are not publicly specified for any of the four examples in the sources accessed. Field-of-view and footprint values are optical geometry, not an instrument envelope, and are not used as dimensions.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Only D-CIXS has a published mass in the sources accessed: about 4.6 kg including its solar monitor [3]. The C1XS, CLASS and SELENE XRS masses are not publicly specified in the sources accessed. Spacecraft masses are not instrument masses and are not used.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not publicly specified for any of the four examples in the sources accessed. No power value is inferred.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar orbital X-ray spectrometer operates in vacuum, under thermal cycling and in a radiation environment, and its detectors must be kept within their operating temperature range. The sources describe SCD detectors as able to operate at relatively warm temperatures without active cooling; one C1XS-related research record describes passive cooling in a range of about -10 C to +5 C [16]. This statement was taken from a search summary of that record, and the primary text was not reviewed. The most important operational constraint is dependence on the Sun: because XRF depends on incident solar X-rays, the lunar signal depends on solar flares and on solar activity during each mission [1][5][7][9]. A solar monitor is therefore an operational requirement, not an optional extra. Viewing geometry also matters: the detectors are described as nadir-pointing, and the ground footprint scales with altitude, so orbit altitude sets the ground scale [1][7].
article.limitations: An X-ray spectrometer does not measure composition directly. It records photons in energy channels, and composition is inferred after calibration and modelling. Element sensitivity depends on energy range and detector efficiency, and light elements may be poorly measured by a given design. The sources accessed do not give a full analysis of these sensitivities for each example. Solar activity limits the observations: C1XS saw about 30 solar X-ray bursts during its mission, limiting global mapping [5]; the SELENE XRS mapping goal was not met [9]; CLASS was designed to use solar flares for some elements [7]. The examples are at different stages: C1XS and SELENE XRS have flight-era records, but their in-flight performance papers were not reviewed in full; CLASS has a 2021 in-flight calibration paper that was not opened in full; D-CIXS's record in this run consists of search summaries rather than full-text reviews. Source conflicts are recorded rather than resolved (see data_quality_notes).

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The four examples are orbiter payloads. Each was integrated into a spacecraft on Earth, launched, transferred to the Moon, inserted into lunar orbit and commissioned. For an orbiter payload the relevant interfaces are spacecraft mounting and alignment, pointing and field-of-view knowledge (the ground footprint depends on viewing direction), thermal control of detectors, power and data handling, and orbit altitude, which sets the ground scale [1][7]. Orbiter X-ray spectrometers are not deployed on the surface. C1XS's deployable door is a protective and calibration feature used during launch and cruise, not a surface deployment mechanism [1]. No lander delivery is described for any of the four examples in the sources accessed, and no compatibility with a named lander is asserted.
transportation_process: Integrate the X-ray spectrometer and its companion solar monitor into the orbiter on Earth, including alignment to the spacecraft's nadir-pointing frame.
Launch the orbiter and transfer it towards the Moon. Launch dates for the examples are given in physical_specifications.examples, with the C1XS discrepancy recorded.
Insert the orbiter into lunar orbit. Orbit altitudes are about 100 km for C1XS [1] and Chandrayaan-2 [14]; the CLASS design paper uses 200 km [7].
Commission the instrument, including calibration against the internal source (C1XS's 55Fe source [1]) and the companion solar monitor [1][3].
Operate the instrument along the orbit during periods of useful solar activity, recording the lunar XRF spectrum and the solar spectrum at the same time [1][7].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not applicable. None of the four examples was deployed on the surface in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: C1XS on Chandrayaan-1, launched in 2008 [2]; D-CIXS on SMART-1 [3]; CLASS on Chandrayaan-2, measuring since 2019 [10]; and the XRS on SELENE (Kaguya), launched in 2007 [8].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a lander, rover or specific spacecraft is asserted beyond the hosting relationships stated in the sources. A new X-ray spectrometer on another spacecraft would need verified mass, dimensions, power, pointing and data-interface documents for that vehicle; several of those values are not publicly specified for the four examples.

article.historical_significance: The four examples form the main family of orbital lunar XRF instruments in the sources accessed. D-CIXS and C1XS are linked by heritage. C1XS's solar monitor and calibration approach are cited as supporting cross-calibration with SELENE XRS [1][9], and CLASS is described as a continuation of C1XS [7]. Together these instruments show how orbital XRF mapping depends on solar activity, detector technology and calibration against the solar spectrum. The sources accessed do not provide one completed global elemental map from a single instrument, so the historical record is best described as a sequence of instrument-level experiments.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: C1XS launch date (22 or 28 October 2008) is unresolved [2][11]. C1XS field of view is 28 by 28 degrees in the ESA archive but 14 degrees FWHM in Howe et al. [1][2]. D-CIXS mass is 4.6 kg in one paper but 5.2 kg for spectrometer and solar monitor in a secondary reference [3][13]; its name is expanded in two ways [3][13]. SMART-1 launch and end dates were not verified. CLASS energy range differs between sources (0.8 to 15 keV, 0.9 to 15 keV, 0.5 to 10 keV) and its orbit altitude differs between the design paper (200 km) and ISRO (100 km) [7][10][14]. The SELENE XRS instrument paper is identified by DOI, but its title and authors were not verified [15]. Power, dimensions and mass are not publicly specified in the sources accessed for most examples, and none is inferred. The Elsevier-hosted Howe et al. (2009) and Icarus (2021) records could not be retrieved in full, so their values come from abstract-level extraction or search summaries.

data_quality_notes: Exact ID, name and category were confirmed against the catalogue: 056, 'X-ray spectrometer', category 3 'Mineralogical and chemical analysis'. Adjacent entries 054 (APXS), 055 (X-ray fluorescence spectrometer), 057 (gamma-ray spectrometer) and 058 (neutron spectrometer) are cross-referenced, not duplicated. The boundary with entry 055 is provisional because the 055 article had not been generated when this article was written.

Image research gap: no image was verified as a direct, rights-checked asset URL in this run. The article and JSON contain no images, and the image registry and section arrays are intentionally empty. This is a research gap rather than a finding that no suitable images exist.
C1XS launch date conflict: ESA PSA gives 22 October 2008 [2]; arXiv:1509.09046 gives 28 October 2008 [11]. Not resolved.
C1XS field-of-view conflict: ESA PSA gives 28 by 28 degrees [2]; Howe et al. (2009) give a 14 degree FWHM field of view with a footprint of about 25 km from 100 km [1]. Not reconciled.
C1XS energy range: ESA PSA gives 0.8 to 20 keV and 85 eV resolution at 1.25 keV [2]; Howe et al. describe efficiency in the 1 to 7 keV band [1]. The full Howe et al. text was not retrieved.

D-CIXS mass conflict: one paper gives about 4.6 kg including the solar monitor [3]; Wikipedia gives 5.2 kg for spectrometer and solar monitor together [13]. Primary value used is 4.6 kg, but the paper was read as a search summary.
D-CIXS name conflict: some sources expand the name as 'Demonstration of a Compact Imaging X-ray Spectrometer' and others as 'Demonstration of a Compact X-ray Spectrometer' [3][13]. Not resolved.

D-CIXS heritage conflict: one search summary associated D-CIXS with the Hayabusa asteroid mission. The other sources place D-CIXS on SMART-1, so the Hayabusa association is not used. The source of that search-summary statement was not verified.

SMART-1 launch and end dates were not verified; the ESA SMART-1 page reviewed does not state them and does not mention D-CIXS [4]. The D-CIXS commissioning statement comes from a 2004 conference abstract summarised in search results [3].
CLASS energy range conflict: 0.8 to 15 keV in one paper [7]; 0.9 to 15 keV in another table [7]; 0.5 to 10 keV in the 2021 in-flight calibration abstract [10]. The primary value needs confirmation.
CLASS orbit conflict: the design paper gives a 200 km orbit for its 25 km ground pixel [7]; ISRO states a 100 km polar orbit for the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter [14]. Not reconciled.

CLASS status: operating since September 2019 per the 2021 Icarus record [10]; no recent mission-status update was found. The ISRO page used for orbit and operational status [14] was cited from article 035 and not re-fetched.

Elsevier-hosted full texts for Howe et al. (2009) and the 2021 Icarus CLASS paper could not be retrieved (redirect records only). The DOI-based citations are retained, but their values come from search summaries.

SELENE XRS: launch date of 14 September 2007 (JST) was fetched directly from JAXA [8]. The XRS instrument paper (DOI 10.1186/BF03352792) has an unverified title and author list [15]. The 16-CCD and 100 cm2 values come from a JpGU 2008 meeting abstract [9] and were read as a search summary. The mapping goal shortfall and cause are as reported in the search summary [9].
SELENE XRS end-of-mission date was not verified in this run.
Chandrayaan-1 end date: RAL Space reports the mission ended in late August 2009 after a major spacecraft failure [5]. The exact end date was not verified against an ISRO or ESA primary source.

Mass, power and dimensions: not publicly specified in the sources accessed for C1XS, CLASS and SELENE XRS, and for D-CIXS power and dimensions. No value is inferred. The only instrument mass recorded is D-CIXS at about 4.6 kg including the solar monitor [3].
Detector cooling statement: the passive-cooling range of about -10 C to +5 C is attributed to a C1XS-related research record [16] read as a search summary; the primary text was not reviewed.

Transportation and compatibility: all four examples are orbiter payloads with no surface delivery in the sources accessed. No lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted. research_status.transportation_compatibility_verified_for_specific_landers is false.
